newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends lower after FOMC holds rates steady.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends lower after FOMC holds rates steady.

text.p: The dollar slumped against major currencies Tuesday after Federal Reserve policy-makers held interest rates steady, prompting fresh concerns about rising inflation, dealers said.

The central bank's monetary policy arm, the Federal Open Market Committee, voted against raising short-term rates, even though a slim majority of analysts had predicted a modest increase at the conclusion of Tuesday's FOMC meeting.
Currency investors who had banked on a rate hike sold dollars on the news, dealers said.

"There's certainly no reason to buy dollars on this news. People are a little worried about the Fed. They're thinking the Fed is a little behind the curve on inflation," said Seth Garrett, director of foreign exchange at CS First Boston.
Many economists at the Fed and in the private sector have warned that the central bank must soon raise interest rates to ease rising inflation pressures in a vigorous economy.

Since domestic inflation erodes the relative purchasing power of the dollar and higher local interest rates tend to strengthen a currency, investors fled into the Japanese yen and European currencies immediately after the FOMC announced its decision Tuesday afternoon.

"It was a knee-jerk reaction to a slightly unexpected situation," said Robert Nelson, managing director of foreign exchange sales at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale. "The market was expecting a quarter-(percentage) point hike in the federal funds rate."

Late Tuesday, the dollar had fallen to 1.5020 German marks from 1.5127 at Monday's close and to 109.05 yen from 109.92 on Monday. The British pound rose to $1.5655 from $1.5564 on Monday. The dollar also fell to 1.2255 Swiss francs from 1.2360, but rose to Canadian $1.3673 from C$1.3667.
The dollar had spent the overnight session trapped in narrow trading ranges as market players delayed investment decisions ahead of the FOMC meeting.

Some dealers blamed politics for delaying a much-needed interest rate increase, with the pressure of presidential and congressional elections only six weeks away seen persuading Fed officials to bide their time.

"The market needed to feel like 25 basis points (added to the current fed funds rate at 5.25 percent) was in and the Fed would do it in front of the election. Now the dollar looks a little bit soft," said Mark Gargano, managing director for foreign exchange at First Union National Bank.
The dollar touched the 1.50-marks level late Tuesday and dealers expected the losses to end either at or just below that key technical level for now.
But with some economists predicting the Fed will keep steady interest rates through the remainder of 1996, investors could continue to sell dollars in coming sessions.
"The dollar could be coming down a little more," Gargano said. "I think there might be a slight problem if the Fed doesn't do anything by the end of the year."

Remaining 1996 FOMC meetings are scheduled for Nov. 13 -- eight days after the election -- and Dec. 17 -- eight days before Christmas. Each would appear to pose timing problems for Fed officials seeking tighter monetary policy, dealers said.
"The Fed is not going to be raising rates for at least a couple of months," said Nelson.
